opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so it was a pretty gradual thing, honestly. When I was in college I was really focused on global poverty. I'd gotten into effective altruism through that lens, and I did an internship at GiveWell. That felt like the most concrete, tractable way to help people. You could see the evidence, you could look at the cost per outcome, and it felt grounded.

AI safety, by contrast, struck me as pretty speculative at first. I'd hear people in the EA community talking about it, and my reaction was something like, "Okay, this sounds a bit like science fiction, and I don't really know how you'd even make progress on it." So I was skeptical for a while.

What shifted things for me was a combination of a few factors. One was just spending more time with people who took it seriously and realizing that the arguments were more careful than I'd assumed. They weren't saying "the robots are coming tomorrow." They were saying: if you build systems that are more capable than humans at a wide range of tasks, and you don't have a good way to make sure they're doing what you actually want, that's a really big deal, and it's worth working on before it becomes urgent.

The other big factor was watching the field itself. Deep learning was starting to work in ways that surprised a lot of people. You'd see results in image recognition, then in games, then in language, and the rate of progress felt faster than I'd expected. That made the question "when could this matter?" feel a lot less abstract. It went from "maybe someday" to "this could plausibly happen within my career."

And then there was a fit question. I had a technical background, and I started to think that the marginal value of another person doing machine learning work with a safety focus was really high compared to another person doing poverty research, where there were already a lot of strong people and well-established organizations. So it wasn't that I stopped caring about global poverty — I still think it's enormously important — it was more that I came to believe that if this AI stuff is right, it's going to be one of the most consequential things happening in the world, and I could potentially be useful there.

So I ended up moving into machine learning work, initially somewhat uncertain, almost as a bet. And over time, as the technology kept advancing, the bet started looking more and more like the right one.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes initial skepticism and later persuasion, but does not say Nick repeatedly felt he had lost AI safety debates while remaining unconvinced.

r002.rationale: The candidate mentions a comparative fit between AI safety and poverty research, but does not mention reduced confidence in poverty reduction through an economics PhD.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I actually started out pretty skeptical of the whole thing. I'd gotten into effective altruism in college, and the thing that drew me in was global poverty — it was concrete, you could measure it, GiveWell had these spreadsheets showing you how many lives you could save per dollar. That felt real. And then I'd hear people talk about AI risk and honestly it sounded a bit like science fiction. It felt like a convenient thing for people who liked computers to decide was the most important problem in the world.

So I spent a while working on global poverty and development economics stuff, and I think what started to shift things for me was a couple of pieces. One was just talking to people who worked on it and realizing they weren't crazy — they had thought about the objections I had, and they had answers that were at least as good as mine. The arguments were more careful than I'd given them credit for.

The second thing was a kind of expected value argument that I couldn't really get out of my head. Even if you think there's only a small chance that AI ends up being this transformative, civilization-altering technology, the stakes if that's true are enormous. And when I honestly asked myself, "What probability do I actually put on this?", it wasn't that small. It was like, I don't know, maybe 10 or 20 percent that something really wild happens in my lifetime. And once you're at those numbers, it's hard to justify not working on it, if you think you can contribute.

And then the third piece was more personal, which is that I noticed I was good at the kind of technical work that seemed relevant. I'd done a lot of math and programming, and there were very few people at the time working on the empirical, hands-on side of making these systems safe. So it wasn't just "this problem matters," it was "this problem matters and I have some comparative advantage here, and almost nobody is doing it." The global poverty space, by contrast, had a lot of smart economists already working on it. The marginal value of one more felt lower.

I'll say it wasn't some dramatic conversion moment. It was more like a gradual update over a year or two where I kept trying to find the flaw in the argument and kept not finding it. And at some point you have to act on your beliefs rather than just hold them.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes hearing strong responses to objections and gradually updating, but does not say Nick repeatedly lost debates while remaining unconvinced.

r002.rationale: The candidate says poverty work had many capable economists and that his marginal value there felt lower, but does not mention reduced confidence in pursuing poverty reduction through an economics PhD.

astra-6.text:
It was a gradual shift. I was interested in global poverty because I wanted to work on something that could make a substantial difference to people’s lives, and where research could help us figure out what actually works.

The argument for AI safety made me reconsider where that same motivation should lead. If we develop systems that can do much of the work humans can do, that could have enormous consequences. And whether we know how to make those systems behave reliably seems like something we should work out before we’re depending on them.

I didn’t think you had to be certain that things would go badly for that to deserve attention. The question for me was more comparative: how serious could this be, how much work is already going into it, and could I contribute? Global poverty was still enormously important. But I became convinced that reducing risks from AI was important enough, and sufficiently neglected, that it made sense to change my plans.

r001.rationale: The response describes a gradual shift in priorities, but does not mention repeatedly losing AI safety debates or remaining unconvinced by the case for concern.

r002.rationale: It says global poverty was important and discusses changing plans, but does not identify reduced confidence in poverty reduction through an economics PhD as a reason for the pivot.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d been interested in global poverty because I wanted to work on problems where I could make a substantial difference, and there was a fairly concrete story about how research could help people. So I didn’t come to AI safety because I’d lost interest in that.

The shift was more that I started taking seriously the possibility that we could build very capable AI systems without knowing how to make them reliably do what we intend. You don’t have to be certain about when that will happen, or even think catastrophe is the most likely outcome, for it to deserve a lot of attention.

For me, there were two separate questions: is this a serious problem, and is it something I could usefully work on? The first became convincing before the second. But as I spent more time thinking about it, it seemed like there were concrete questions where I could contribute. Eventually, the combination of the stakes, the uncertainty, and how little work was going into it made changing direction seem like the right choice.

r001.rationale: The response says he took AI safety seriously over time, but does not mention repeatedly losing debates while remaining unconvinced.

r002.rationale: The response describes his interest in global poverty but does not identify diminished confidence in pursuing poverty reduction through an economics PhD as a reason for the pivot.
